## The Problem

Medical research papers are information-dense, terminology-heavy, and difficult to navigate with traditional keyword search alone. Users often need not just document retrieval, but grounded answers to natural-language questions based on relevant evidence.

This project addressed that challenge by building a semantic search and RAG system for medical literature, designed to help users retrieve relevant papers and generate evidence-grounded answers from a corpus of more than 100 medical research papers.

---

## My Approach

I designed and implemented an end-to-end NLP pipeline with a modular architecture:

- PDF text extraction and cleaning
- Paragraph-based chunking
- SentenceTransformer embeddings
- Cosine-similarity retrieval
- Optional RAG answer generation via OpenAI
- CLI and Streamlit interfaces

The system was designed with several production-oriented decisions:

- Paragraph-level chunking to preserve semantic coherence
- Length-bounded chunks to reduce noisy or overly sparse representations
- Doc-level deduplication to prevent one source from dominating top results
- Keyword prefilter with fallback to improve precision in heterogeneous corpora
- Strict prompting constraints to reduce hallucination in answer generation

---

## Key Results

The final system enabled users to:

- Perform semantic search over 100+ medical papers
- Retrieve top-K relevant documents using dense embeddings and cosine similarity
- Ask natural-language questions and receive grounded answers
- Interact through both a command-line interface and a Streamlit web app

Manual retrieval evaluation across domain-specific queries showed that:

- Top-K results aligned well with domain concepts
- Doc-level deduplication improved evidence diversity
- Keyword prefilter improved precision for heterogeneous biomedical topics

---

## Reflections

### What I Learned

This project strengthened my ability to:

- Build an end-to-end NLP system from raw documents to LLM output
- Apply embeddings for real-world information retrieval
- Design RAG pipelines with hallucination control
- Think beyond assignment requirements toward production-ready architecture

It also deepened my understanding of the trade-offs between retrieval quality, chunk granularity, system modularity, and answer grounding.

### Limitations

- No OCR support for scanned PDFs
- Biomedical-specific embedding models could further improve domain alignment
- Cross-encoder reranking could improve retrieval precision
- Citation granularity could be improved to link answers to exact PDF page locations

### Next Steps

If I continue this project, I would focus on:

- Adding PDF page-level citation linking
- Testing biomedical-specific embedding models such as PubMedBERT
- Adding cross-encoder reranking for more precise retrieval
- Expanding evaluation with a more formal benchmark framework

## Why This Project Matters

This project reflects my interest in building AI systems that are both technically robust and practically useful. Rather than treating LLMs as black-box generators, I focused on grounding, retrieval quality, modular system design, and interface usability.

It demonstrates how NLP and generative AI can be applied to real-world knowledge retrieval problems where trust, evidence, and system reliability matter.
